summary: John Drake worked in Indology and religious studies. He studied at Regent's Park College and the University of Oxford (M.A.). He was Vice-Principal and Professor of Theology and Ethics at Serampore College (1910–1926) and served at Saharanpur Theological Seminary until 1933.
John Drew Bate was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Regent's Park College from circa 1861 to 1865. He served as a member of the Baptist Missionary Society from 1865 to 1897.

John E. Cort is an Indologist and scholar of religious studies. He earned a BA from the University of Wisconsin-Madison and an AM from Harvard University. In approximately 1992, he became a professor at Denison University.

John F. Richards worked in Indology and history/archaeology. He studied at the University of New Hampshire and UC Berkeley. Richards held faculty posts at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (1968–1977) and Duke University (circa 1977–2007).

John Faithfull Fleet worked in Indology and history/archaeology. Educated at Merchant Taylors' School and UCL, he studied under Theodor Goldstücker. A civil servant in India (1865–1897), he served as Government Epigraphist (1883–1886) and Honorary Secretary of the Royal Asiatic Society (1906–1917).
John Firminger Duthie served as Superintendent of the Saharanpur Botanical Garden from circa 1876 to 1903 and as Director of the Botanical Survey of India from circa 1891 to 1903.

John Forbes Royle was an Indologist who studied at Addiscombe Military Seminary and the University of Edinburgh. He served as Superintendent of Saharanpur Botanical Garden (1823–1831), Professor at King's College London (1837–1856), and curator at the India Office (circa 1838–1858).

John Forbes White Youngson worked in linguistics and Indology. He earned an M.A. (1873) and D.D. (1893) from the University of Aberdeen, and served as a Church of Scotland missionary from 1875 to 1907.

John Frederick Browne worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Exeter College, Oxford (circa 1853–1855) and the East India Company College (circa 1855–1856), later taking a post with the Bengal Civil Service in 1858.
John Frederick Dickson was a scholar of Buddhist studies and Indology. He was educated at Westminster School and Christ Church, Oxford, completing his B.A. in 1859.

John Garrett worked in Indology and linguistics. In 1858, he became the first director of the Central College of Bangalore, and in 1871 served as Director of Public Instruction for the Department of Public Instruction, Mysore.

John George Woodroffe worked in Indology and religious studies. Educated at University College, Oxford, and under Sivachandra Vidyarnava, he served as a Calcutta High Court judge (circa 1904–1922) and Reader in Indian Law at Oxford (1923–1930).

John Gombojab Hangin worked in linguistics and Iranian/Central Asian studies. Educated at Hokkaido, Columbia, and Indiana University, he held posts at Johns Hopkins, Georgetown, Columbia, and UC Berkeley before serving as full professor at Indiana University Bloomington (1965–1989).
John Graham Drummond worked in Indology and linguistics. He earned a B.A. (circa 1906) and Ph.D. (1939) from Christ's College, Cambridge, where he was also appointed Lecturer in Bengali in 1936.

John Greenfield Leonard was a scholar of history, archaeology, and Indology. He earned degrees from Stanford and the University of Wisconsin-Madison, later holding posts at Wisconsin (1967) and the University of California, San Diego (1968–1973).

John Griffiths worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He studied at the Royal College of Art, worked at the Victoria and Albert Museum, and served as Professor at Sir Jamsetjee Jeejebhoy School of Art (1865) and Principal of the National College of Arts (circa 1880–1895).
John H. Berthrong is a scholar of Sinology, philosophy, and religious studies who studied under graduate supervisor Alfonso Verdu. He held an affiliation at Boston University attested in 1996.
John Hay, who worked in Sinology, earned an M.A. from the University of Aberdeen in 1833. He served as a Fellow at the University of Madras from 1888 to 1889 and taught Chüan-ying Yen.

John Henry Hutton was an Indologist and historian educated at Chigwell School, Worcester College, and Oxford (D.Sc. 1921). He served in the Indian Civil Service (circa 1909–1937) and was William Wyse Professor of Social Anthropology at Cambridge (1936–1950).

John Henry Piet worked in Indology, philosophy, and religious studies. Educated at Hope College, Western Theological Seminary, Princeton, Hartford, and Columbia (Ph.D.), he served as Professor of English Bible and Mission at Western Theological Seminary from 1960 to 1984.
